lessonTitle: Endocrine, Haematological and Genetic Disease in Children: Growth, Anaemia and Syndromes

blocks.text: A previously dry 9-year-old has wet the bed every night for a fortnight, drinks litres of water, and has lost weight despite eating well. This morning he is vomiting, breathing deeply and fast, and has abdominal pain. A fingerprick glucose will give the diagnosis in seconds, and recognising the pattern early is what keeps him out of intensive care.

blocks.markdown: This unit brings together four groups of conditions that a paediatrician must recognise: **type 1 diabetes** and **congenital hypothyroidism** (endocrine), **sickle cell disease** and **childhood leukaemia** (haematological), and **common chromosomal syndromes** (genetic). A shared theme is that early recognition changes outcomes: neurodevelopment in hypothyroidism, survival in leukaemia, and infection prevention in sickle cell disease.

blocks.title: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM)
blocks.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency. Without insulin, glucose cannot enter cells and the body breaks down fat, producing ketones. It is the commonest form of diabetes in children in the UK.

blocks.markdown: **Presentation of T1DM.** Hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal threshold, so glucose spills into urine and causes an osmotic diuresis. This explains the classic **polyuria** (including new bedwetting), **polydipsia**, and **weight loss**, with tiredness, blurred vision and recurrent infections such as candidiasis. About a quarter of children present in **diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**: dehydration, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing, ketotic breath, drowsiness and shock. Diagnosis in a symptomatic child is by capillary or laboratory glucose and ketones, using current national diagnostic criteria. DKA is managed in hospital with careful fluids and intravenous insulin under a national or local protocol (for example the BSPED guideline); cerebral oedema is a rare but serious complication, which is why fluid and insulin regimens are not improvised. Check all treatment details against current BSPED/NICE/local guidance.

blocks.title: Estimating dehydration from weight (teaching calculation)
blocks.prompt: A girl newly presenting with DKA weighed 32 kg at her last clinic visit a month ago and weighs 30.4 kg today. Estimate the percentage weight loss and say how it informs assessment of dehydration.

steps.text: Weight lost equals previous weight minus current weight.
Percentage loss relative to the previous weight.

Interpretation: some weight loss in DKA is lost tissue, so true fluid deficit cannot be read from weight alone. Clinical signs (capillary refill, heart rate, mucous membranes, conscious level) and current guideline protocols decide fluid management.

blocks.answer: 5% weight loss; use as supporting information only, with clinical assessment and the local DKA protocol deciding fluids.

blocks.markdown: **Congenital hypothyroidism** (thyroid hormone deficiency present at birth) is most often due to a thyroid gland that is absent, small or in the wrong place (dysgenesis). Thyroid hormone is essential for brain development in the first years of life, so untreated disease causes severe intellectual disability. Signs in the first weeks are often subtle: **prolonged jaundice**, poor feeding, constipation, hypotonia, a large tongue, a hoarse cry, umbilical hernia, cool dry skin and a large posterior fontanelle. Because clinical detection is unreliable, the UK **newborn blood spot screen** measures thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which is raised in primary hypothyroidism. Treatment is lifelong levothyroxine started as early as possible, with monitoring and dosing set by specialists (check against current BNFc guidance).

blocks.caption: Presentations of endocrine disease in this unit
rows: Any age; peaks in childhood and adolescence
Prolonged jaundice, constipation, hypotonia, large tongue
Newborn blood spot TSH, then thyroid function tests

blocks.markdown:
**Sickle cell disease (SCD)** is an autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy (HbSS, or HbS with another variant). Deoxygenated HbS polymerises and distorts red cells, causing haemolysis and vaso-occlusion. When both parents are carriers (sickle cell trait, HbAS), each pregnancy has a **1 in 4 (25%)** chance of an affected child, 1 in 2 chance of a carrier and 1 in 4 chance of an unaffected non-carrier. Complications to recognise:

- **Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis**, and **dactylitis** in infants (swollen painful hands and feet).
- **Acute chest syndrome**: chest pain, fever, hypoxia, new infiltrate; potentially life-threatening.
- **Splenic sequestration**: sudden pallor, left upper quadrant mass, falling haemoglobin and shock in young children.
- **Aplastic crisis** (often parvovirus B19), **stroke**, and **overwhelming infection** from functional hyposplenism with encapsulated organisms.

Prevention includes penicillin prophylaxis and immunisations as set out in the UKHSA Green Book and local protocols, and transcranial Doppler screening for stroke risk in children as per specialist guidance.

blocks.title: Fever in a child with sickle cell disease
blocks.prompt: A 4-year-old with HbSS arrives with a temperature of 38.6 C, looking mildly tired but alert. His parents note he missed a penicillin dose. His mother asks whether paracetamol and review tomorrow is acceptable.

steps.text: Mechanism: functional hyposplenism impairs clearance of encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus, so even well-looking children can develop septicaemia within hours.
Action: fever in sickle cell disease is a medical emergency needing urgent hospital assessment, blood cultures and prompt parenteral antibiotics, following local sickle cell guidance.
Look for other causes and complications: chest signs, pain, pallor, spleen size, and check blood count and oxygen saturation.
Prevention counselling: adherence to penicillin prophylaxis and immunisation, and a written plan for fever.

blocks.answer: No: this is an emergency needing same-day hospital assessment, cultures and early antibiotics.

blocks.markdown: **Childhood leukaemia.** Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the commonest childhood cancer; acute myeloid leukaemia is less common. Malignant blasts crowd out normal marrow, causing **anaemia** (pallor, tiredness), **thrombocytopenia** (bruising, petechiae, bleeding), and **neutropenia** (infections, fever). Other features include bone pain or limping, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and, in some, a mediastinal mass or testicular and central nervous system involvement. A full blood count and film may show anaemia, low platelets, and abnormal white count with blasts. Suspicion triggers **urgent same-day** referral to paediatric haematology for marrow examination; do not start steroids before specialist advice because this can obscure the diagnosis.

blocks.title: Unexplained bruising plus pallor needs an urgent blood count
blocks.text: Combinations such as pallor, petechiae, bone pain, persistent fever or hepatosplenomegaly should prompt an immediate full blood count and film, not watchful waiting.

blocks.caption: Common chromosomal syndromes
rows: Hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, flat facial profile
Congenital heart disease (especially atrioventricular septal defect), duodenal atresia, hearing and vision problems, hypothyroidism, learning disability, leukaemia risk
Short stature, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, lymphoedema
Coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, ovarian failure, renal anomalies
Tall stature, small firm testes, often diagnosed late
Hypogonadism and infertility, learning and language difficulties
Severe growth restriction, clenched overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet
Severe heart disease; most do not survive infancy

blocks.title: Think of the system, then the syndrome
blocks.text: Each syndrome has predictable organ involvement. In a baby with Down syndrome, look for heart disease and thyroid problems; in a girl with short stature, think of Turner syndrome and check blood pressure and the heart.

points: Type 1 diabetes presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss or DKA; congenital hypothyroidism is detected by newborn TSH screening and needs prompt levothyroxine to protect brain development.

Sickle cell disease causes pain crises, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, stroke and serious infection, so fever is an emergency; leukaemia presents with marrow failure features and needs urgent blood count and referral.
Chromosomal syndromes such as trisomy 21 and Turner syndrome have predictable associated problems that guide screening and follow-up.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has three weeks of thirst, frequent urination and weight loss. A fingerprick glucose is markedly raised and urine ketones are positive. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing insulin deficiency
Peripheral insulin resistance with high insulin levels

questions.correctOptionText: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing insulin deficiency

distractorRationale.a: Correct: absolute insulin deficiency causes hyperglycaemia and ketosis.
distractorRationale.b: Insulin resistance describes type 2 diabetes and rarely produces ketosis at this speed.
distractorRationale.c: Cushing syndrome causes weight gain and a different picture.
distractorRationale.d: Growth hormone deficiency causes short stature, not hyperglycaemia.

questions.explanation: Osmotic symptoms with ketonuria and weight loss in a child reflect absolute insulin deficiency from autoimmune beta cell destruction. Ketones show fat is being broken down because glucose cannot be used.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old term infant has persisting jaundice, feeds slowly, is constipated and has a protruding tongue and an umbilical hernia. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prolonged jaundice, constipation, macroglossia and hernia are classic.
distractorRationale.b: T1DM presents with osmotic symptoms, rarely in the first weeks.
distractorRationale.c: Pyloric stenosis presents with projectile vomiting, not this picture.
distractorRationale.d: Hirschsprung disease does not explain prolonged jaundice and macroglossia.

questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone deficiency slows many systems, causing prolonged jaundice, constipation, poor feeding and hypotonia. Early treatment protects neurodevelopment, which is why newborn screening measures TSH.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with sickle cell disease develops sudden pallor, lethargy and a tender enlarging mass in the left upper quadrant; haemoglobin has fallen sharply from baseline. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: red cells pool in the spleen, causing enlargement and falling haemoglobin.
distractorRationale.b: Acute chest syndrome has respiratory features.
distractorRationale.c: Dactylitis is painful swollen hands and feet.

questions.explanation: In young children with sickle cell disease the spleen can trap blood, causing a rapid fall in haemoglobin, a large spleen and shock. It needs urgent resuscitation and transfusion under specialist guidance.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has 3 weeks of pallor, leg pain causing limping, and new bruises. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. A blood count shows low haemoglobin and platelets with a raised white cell count. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Same-day referral to paediatric haematology without starting steroids
Oral iron and review in 4 weeks
Start prednisolone for presumed immune thrombocytopenia

questions.correctOptionText: Same-day referral to paediatric haematology without starting steroids

distractorRationale.a: Correct: suspected leukaemia needs urgent specialist assessment and steroids can obscure the diagnosis.
distractorRationale.b: Iron does not treat marrow failure.
distractorRationale.c: Growing pains do not cause cytopenias or organomegaly.
distractorRationale.d: Steroids before diagnosis can mask leukaemia.

questions.explanation: Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, bone pain and hepatosplenomegaly suggest marrow infiltration by leukaemia. Urgent haematology referral allows blood film review and marrow examination, and steroids are avoided before diagnosis.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a webbed neck, swollen hands and feet and a systolic murmur with weak femoral pulses. Which karyotype is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Turner syndrome with coarctation of the aorta.
distractorRationale.c: Trisomy 21 features differ and the typical lesion is AVSD.

questions.explanation: Webbed neck, lymphoedema of hands and feet and weak femoral pulses in a girl suggest Turner syndrome with coarctation of the aorta. Karyotype confirms the diagnosis.

questions.stem: True or false: a child with Down syndrome needs screening for congenital heart disease, hearing and vision problems and thyroid dysfunction.
questions.explanation: These problems are common in trisomy 21 and are treatable, so structured screening and follow-up are standard. Early detection supports development and prevents avoidable harm.

questions.stem: Two healthy parents are both carriers of sickle cell trait (HbAS). What is the probability, as a percentage, that any one of their children has sickle cell disease (HbSS)?
questions.explanation: Autosomal recessive inheritance from two carriers gives HbAA 25%, HbAS 50% and HbSS 25%. Each pregnancy is independent, so the risk is 25% every time.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes weighed 24.0 kg at a school check three weeks ago and weighs 22.2 kg now. Calculate his percentage weight loss relative to the earlier weight.
questions.explanation: Weight lost is 24.0 minus 22.2, which is 1.8 kg. Dividing by 24.0 gives 0.075, or 7.5%. This is a measure of the catabolic state and not a direct estimate of fluid deficit.

questions.stem: Explain the mechanism of the classic symptoms of newly presenting type 1 diabetes and describe the features of diabetic ketoacidosis.
markingGuide: Insulin deficiency causes hyperglycaemia exceeding the renal threshold
Glycosuria causes osmotic diuresis: polyuria, nocturia or bedwetting, then polydipsia
Weight loss from catabolism of fat and protein
DKA: ketone production causes acidosis, deep sighing breathing, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, drowsiness, shock
Managed in hospital under a national or local protocol; cerebral oedema is a serious complication
questions.explanation: Without insulin, cells cannot use glucose so the body breaks down fat, and high glucose causes an osmotic diuresis. Ketones are acidic, producing the respiratory compensation and gastrointestinal symptoms of DKA.

questions.stem: Describe three complications of sickle cell disease in children and explain why fever is an emergency in this group.
markingGuide: Any three from vaso-occlusive crisis, dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis, stroke
A brief description of the presentation or mechanism of each
Functional hyposplenism impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus
Rapid progression to septicaemia, so urgent assessment, cultures and parenteral antibiotics
Prevention by penicillin prophylaxis and immunisation per UKHSA Green Book and local guidance
questions.explanation: Repeated sickling infarcts the spleen so children are prone to overwhelming infection. Fever must therefore be treated as a medical emergency regardless of how well the child looks.
